questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: The two-ray model of a film
questions.learningObjective: state that a film's reflected light is the sum of two reflections from its two surfaces
questions.stem: A thin transparent film lies on a flat surface and is illuminated from the air above. What two contributions make up the light reflected from the film?

options.text: One reflected from the top surface of the film and one from its bottom surface
One reflected from the top surface and one transmitted out through the far side
options.misconception: treats light going the wrong way through the film as part of the reflection

options.text: One reflected at each end of the film, from the light entering at opposite sides
options.misconception: doubles the beam rather than counting the two surfaces of one beam

options.text: One from the top surface and one from the metal behind the film, by induction
options.misconception: invents a conductor where the problem describes only a transparent film

questions.explanation: A beam that meets the film is partly reflected at the top surface and partly refracted into the film, where it reaches the bottom surface, is partly reflected there, and only then leaves upwards. Those two upward beams overlap and interfere, which is the whole of the physics of a coloured film. Because the second beam has travelled down and back up through the film as well as along the extra distance between the two reflecting points, it arrives with an optical path difference of 2 n t cos r, and to that must be added any phase change the reflections themselves produce. A film a few hundred nanometres thick is therefore not a single reflecting surface but a pair of them, and treating it as one surface is the commonest reason for predicting that a film cannot produce colour at all. The distinction also explains why the colour depends on the angle of view, since cos r changes with angle, while the thickness stays fixed.
questions.hint: Count the places at which the incident beam can turn back towards the observer.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Phase change on reflection from a denser medium
questions.learningObjective: state that reflection from a less dense medium adds half a wavelength of phase change
questions.stem: Light travelling in air meets a surface of a denser transparent material. What happens to the phase of the reflected wave compared with the incident one?

options.text: It is unchanged, since reflection cannot alter the phase of a wave
options.misconception: denies the phase step, which is a real and observable change of sign

options.text: It is unchanged in amplitude but advanced by a quarter of a wavelength
options.misconception: gives the wrong fraction, since the step is half a wavelength rather than a quarter

options.text: It is reversed, a change of half a wavelength, because the wave reflects off a stiffer medium
It is delayed by a whole wavelength, since the wave has to cross the boundary twice
options.misconception: invokes a delay rather than a sign change, which is a different phenomenon

questions.explanation: Light is an electromagnetic wave, and the electric field of an electromagnetic wave pushes on the charges it meets. Reflection from a medium of lower refractive index than the one the wave is in, which is the optically denser case, drives those charges in the same sense as the incident field, and the sum at the surface is a field turned inside out. That is a phase change of half a wavelength, or a sign reversal, with no change of amplitude to first order. Reflection from a less dense medium has the opposite sense of charge motion and no such reversal. This is the single most consequential detail in thin-film work, because the two beams in a film typically have one reversal and not two, so the conditions for a bright and a dark reflection come out reversed relative to the naive reading of the path difference alone. It is also why an anti-reflection coating is a quarter of a wavelength thick: the reversal supplies the half wavelength that the thickness does not.
questions.hint: Ask which way the charges in the new medium are driven by the arriving field.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Thinnest film giving a dark reflection
questions.learningObjective: apply the one-reversal dark condition to find the thinnest film thickness
questions.stem: A film of refractive index 1.38 with air on both sides is viewed in reflected light of wavelength 550 nm in air. What is the thinnest film thickness that reflects no light at all, in nanometres? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Air into film is a step up in index and reverses the wave, while film into air does not, so the two reflected beams already differ by half a wavelength before any travel. For the total difference to be a whole number of wavelengths, and so for the two to cancel, the extra optical path must be a half wavelength: 2 n t = lambda over 2, giving t = 550 nm / (2 x 1.38) = 199.3 nm. The two routes agree. Inside the film the wavelength is shortened to 550 / 1.38 = 398.6 nm, and a film half a wavelength thick inside the film is 199.3 nm in air, which is the same number. The common wrong answer is 99.6 nm, the quarter-wave figure that applies to a bright reflection; and 100 nm, from using the wavelength outside the film, is wrong by the index. Sanity check: a film thinner than this reflects very little, which is why an oil film on water looks black where it is thinnest, and the thickness is of the right order since visible wavelengths are a few hundred nanometres.
questions.hint: There is one reversal between the two reflected beams, so ask what extra path is needed to complete the half wavelength it already provides.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Thinnest film giving a bright reflection
questions.learningObjective: apply the one-reversal bright condition to find the thinnest film thickness
questions.stem: Reflected light of wavelength 550 nm in air falls on a film of refractive index 1.38 that has air on both sides. At what thickness, in nanometres, is the reflection strongest? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: With one reversal between the two beams, the strongest reflection needs the two to arrive in step overall, so the reversal must be cancelled by the travel difference. The extra optical path must therefore be an odd half wavelength, and for the thinnest film, 2 n t = lambda over 4, so t = 550 nm / (4 x 1.38) = 99.6 nm. The same figure follows from the wavelength inside the film, which is 550 / 1.38 = 398.6 nm, of which a quarter is 99.6 nm in air. Note the pairing with the previous item: the thickness for a bright reflection is exactly half that for a dark one, which is a quick way to check any such calculation, and the two add to the dark thickness because the two conditions are complementary. The value also sits below the 199.3 nm dark thickness, as it must, and both are of the order of a fraction of a wavelength, which is why such films are coloured at all.
questions.hint: One reversal is present, so the extra optical path must supply the other half wavelength.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: A film on a denser substrate reverses the conditions
questions.learningObjective: apply the two-reversal conditions for a film on a denser substrate
questions.stem: A film of refractive index 1.20 is deposited on glass of refractive index 1.52 and viewed in reflection under light of wavelength 550 nm in air. At what thickness, in nanometres, is this coating brightest, if it is to work at that single wavelength? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Both reflections now reverse, because the first step is air into film and the second is film into glass, and both go up in index. Two reversals together contribute a whole wavelength, which changes nothing, so the conditions swap over from the free-standing case: a bright reflection now needs the extra optical path to be a whole number of wavelengths rather than an odd half. For the thinnest film that is 2 n t = lambda, so t = 550 nm / (2 x 1.20) = 229.2 nm. In terms of optical thickness the answer is 1.20 x 229.2 = 275 nm, exactly half a wavelength, which is the statement of the condition. This is why a quarter-wave coating works only where it is bounded by media whose indices straddle its own: the design of an anti-reflection coating relies on deliberately arranging one reversal, and an unnoticed second one turns the coating into a quarter-wave plate of the wrong sign.
questions.hint: Count the reversals first; two of them cancel, which swaps the bright and dark conditions over.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Index of a wedge film from its fringe spacing
questions.learningObjective: recover a film's index from the spacing of its wedge fringes
questions.stem: A wedge-shaped film lies between two glass blocks and is illuminated with light of wavelength 600 nm in air. Consecutive dark fringes in reflection appear where the film is 0.30 micrometres thick and then 0.51 micrometres thick. What is the refractive index of the film? Report the number only.

options.text: 2.86, from the wavelength divided by the fringe spacing with the factor of two dropped
options.misconception: drops the factor of two in the thin-film condition, doubling the index

options.text: 1.43, from the wavelength over twice the spacing between dark fringes
0.714, from the wavelength over four times the spacing between dark fringes
options.misconception: divides by four where the condition calls for two, halving the index

options.text: 0.175, from inverting the ratio and dividing by a further two
options.misconception: inverts the whole relation and then halves, which is two slips at once

questions.explanation: In a wedge the thickness grows steadily, so a fringe of constant condition marks a constant increment of optical thickness, and consecutive dark fringes are separated by lambda over 2 n whatever the local thickness is. Here that increment is 0.51 - 0.30 = 0.21 micrometres, so 2 n x 0.21 micrometres = 600 nm and n = 600 / (2 x 210) = 1.43. The consistency check works on the difference, as the condition does: 2 x 1.43 x 0.21 micrometres = 600 nm, exactly one wavelength, which is what makes the two fringes consecutive ones of the same kind. The absolute optical thicknesses are 857 nm and 1457 nm, a difference of 600 nm. A figure of 1.43 is unremarkable for a solid film, which is the sort of number a thin-film measurement is normally made to find. The 0.714 answer is the same relation with a four where a two belongs, and the inverting slip in the last option is worth watching for because both of its factors are wrong in the same direction.
questions.hint: Consecutive dark fringes differ by one half wavelength of optical path, so work with the difference in thickness.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Fringe spacing in an air wedge
questions.learningObjective: find the fringe spacing of an air wedge from its angle and the wavelength
questions.stem: Two glass blocks are pressed together at one end so that the air gap between them opens out linearly, reaching 1.0e-4 radians. The wedge is viewed in reflection with light of wavelength 600 nm in air. What is the spacing between successive dark fringes, in millimetres? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The gap thickness at a distance x from the contact is t = x times the wedge angle, so the optical path between the two reflected beams is 2 x tan(alpha) and, for a dark fringe, that has to change by one whole wavelength from one fringe to the next. Setting 2 alpha dx = lambda gives dx = 600 nm / (2 x 1.0e-4) = 3.0 mm. The count over a measured length is the independent check: at 30 mm from the contact the gap is 30e-3 x 1.0e-4 = 3.0e-6 m, the optical path there is 6.0e-6 m, and 6.0e-6 / 600e-9 is exactly 10 wavelengths, so ten fringe intervals separate the contact from 30 mm, and 30 mm divided by 10 gives the same 3.0 mm spacing. Notice that the spacing is inversely proportional to the wedge angle, so a steeper wedge shows its fringes closer together, and that it is the two-way path that supplies the factor of two, which is the usual slip.
questions.hint: The gap grows linearly with distance, and the optical path is twice the gap.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Radius of a Newton's ring
questions.learningObjective: obtain a Newton's ring radius from the radius of curvature and the order
questions.stem: A plano-convex lens of radius of curvature 0.500 m rests on a flat glass plate and is viewed in reflected light of wavelength 589.3 nm in air. What is the radius of the fifth dark ring, in millimetres? Report the number only.

options.text: 1.214 mm, from the square root of the order times the wavelength times the radius
0.858 mm, from a square root taken of half the product inside it
options.misconception: divides inside the square root by two, which halves the radius rather than the area

options.text: 0.0015 mm, from the product without the square root the geometry requires
options.misconception: drops the square root, so the result is an area expressed as a length

options.text: 2.428 mm, from doubling the radius to quote a diameter as if it were a radius
options.misconception: confuses a diameter with a radius, which is exactly a factor of two

questions.explanation: A spherical surface of radius R meeting a flat one gives a gap of t = r squared over 2R at radius r, so the two-way optical path is r squared over R. Setting that equal to the order times a wavelength for a dark ring gives r = the square root of m lambda R, and with m = 5, lambda = 589.3 nm and R = 0.500 m that is the square root of 5 x 589.3e-9 x 0.500, which is 1.473e-6 square metres, so r = 1.214 mm. The scaling is the check: the first dark ring sits at the square root of 5.893e-7 x 0.500 = 5.43e-4 m, or 0.543 mm, and the fifth must be the square root of five times that, a factor of 2.236, which returns 1.214 mm. Ring radii therefore grow as the square root of the order, not linearly, and a spacing measured between neighbouring rings narrows steadily as you move outward from the contact.
questions.hint: The geometry of a sphere gives the gap as the square of the radius over twice the radius of curvature.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why the centre of a Newton's pattern is dark
questions.learningObjective: explain that the two reflected beams cancel exactly at the point of contact
questions.stem: A Newton's rings pattern is viewed in reflected light with a plano-convex lens resting on a glass plate. What is the state of the pattern at the point where the two surfaces touch?

options.text: Bright, since the two reflected beams arrive in step and add together
options.misconception: claims addition where the single reversal makes them cancel

options.text: Dark, since the two reflected beams there are exactly out of step and cancel
Absent, since a film of zero thickness reflects no light at all
options.misconception: denies reflection at a vanishing thickness, which is the interesting case

options.text: Unfocused, since the lens curvature puts the contact outside the depth of field
options.misconception: brings in an optical alignment problem that does not set the brightness

questions.explanation: At the point of contact the two reflected beams have no path difference at all, since they come from the same piece of glass, so the only thing separating them is the single reversal that reflection from the less dense of the two glass surfaces produces. That is exactly half a wavelength, so the two cancel and the centre is dark. The prediction is sharp enough to be tested: rest the lens down properly and the centre is black, but press the contact slightly, which squeezes in a wedge and gives a small air gap, and the centre brightens at once, because the extra path then supplies the missing half wavelength. That test is also the practical way of telling a real contact from an apparent one, and it is why a Newton's rings apparatus is wiped clean before use, since a speck of dust at the contact lifts the lens and puts the whole pattern out of step. The third option is the natural wrong guess, and the interesting fact is that a vanishingly thin film reflects nothing rather than everything.
questions.hint: With no path difference at all, the only phase difference left is the one produced by the reflections themselves.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why soap bubbles show colour bands
questions.learningObjective: explain that colours on a soap film come from its draining thickness changing
questions.stem: A soap bubble at the top of a frame turns black within seconds, then shows bright bands of colour that drift downwards. What is happening to the film?

options.text: The film is thickest at the top, so only one colour is reflected from the top region
options.misconception: places the thick region at the top, whereas drainage makes the top the thinnest

options.text: The light inside the bubble has become polarised, so a polarizer is doing the colouring
options.misconception: requires a polarizer that is not present, since the colours appear to the naked eye

options.text: The bubble is emitting its own light, and the emission changes colour as the film thins
options.misconception: confuses reflected interference with emission, which is a different process entirely

options.text: The film thins as it drains, so the thickness that reflects one colour replaces another

questions.explanation: A bubble is a liquid film, and gravity drains the liquid down, so the film is thinnest at the top and thickest at the bottom. The thickness at any point therefore changes continuously, and since a given colour is reflected strongly only where the two-way optical path brings that wavelength into step, the band of reflected colour drifts downwards as the thickness there passes through the value that selects it. The black patch at the top is the limit of the same argument: there the film is thinner than a fraction of a wavelength, the two reflected beams are out of step by the single reversal alone, and they cancel, leaving nothing to reflect. The arithmetic shows the scale. For a film of index 1.33, one quarter of a wavelength of 550 nm corresponds to 550 / (4 x 1.33) = 103 nm, and 650 nm needs 122 nm, so the two colours are reinforced at thicknesses differing by under 20 nm, which is why the bands are narrow and numerous. Two pale reflections interfering is the whole mechanism, and no polarizer is involved.
questions.hint: Ask what changes with time at each point on the film, and what sets the colour at a given thickness.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: What a Michelson interferometer compares
questions.learningObjective: state that a Michelson interferometer compares two optical paths to the same detector
questions.stem: A Michelson interferometer is laid out as follows. A source S on the left sends light to a beam splitter B mounted at 45 degrees. One beam travels right from B to a fixed mirror M1 and back. The other travels up from B to a mirror M2 on a sliding mount and back. Both returning beams pass back through B, which sends them along a common path to the detector D, where the circle pattern of light and dark rings is observed. What is being compared when a fringe changes at D?

options.text: The two optical path lengths from the source, out to the two mirrors and back to D
The two wavelengths of the two beams, since the mirrors select different colours
options.misconception: supposes the mirrors act as colour filters, which they do not

options.text: The two angles of the returning beams, since the splitter bends them apart
options.misconception: confuses the two beam directions, which the splitter recombines rather than separates

options.text: The two phase changes at the beam splitter, which differ between the two passes
options.misconception: invents a difference at the splitter, which affects both beams the same way

questions.explanation: The splitter creates two beams that travel different routes and are then brought back to the same detector, so every fringe that appears at D records the difference between those two optical path lengths. In the arrangement described, the beam that goes to M1 travels a fixed route while the beam that goes to M2 travels one that can be lengthened by sliding M2, and a fringe appears or disappears at D whenever the difference changes by one wavelength. Everything else in the instrument is arranged so that the two beams see the same surroundings, which is why the splitter is compensated with a plate of glass matched to the beamsplitter material: otherwise the beam that passed through the splitter on the way out would have acquired an extra delay that the returning beam did not, and the fringes would sit at a shifted position rather than tracking the true mirror motion. The pattern is of rings because the path difference varies across the field of view, one fringe thickness across each ring.
questions.hint: Both beams end at the same detector, so what can be compared is the route each one took to get there.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Fringes counted for a mirror movement
questions.learningObjective: count the fringes that pass when one mirror of an interferometer is moved
questions.stem: In the Michelson arrangement described, one mirror is moved 0.0200 mm along the beam while the other stays fixed. With light of wavelength 5.00e-7 m in air, how many fringes pass the detector? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Moving a mirror by d lengthens one route by d on the way out and by d on the way back, so the optical path difference changes by twice the movement, and a fringe passes whenever that change reaches one wavelength. The number of fringes is therefore 2 d over lambda, which is 2 x 2.0e-5 / 5.00e-7 = 80. The two routes through the arithmetic give the same result: the total optical change is 4.0e-5 m, and dividing that by the 5.00e-7 m wavelength gives 80. The factor of two is the whole content of the problem, and omitting it gives 40, which is the most common slip in using this instrument. A useful cross-check on the size: 2.0e-5 m is 40 wavelengths of travel in each direction, so the motion is slow enough for the fringes to be followed one at a time by eye, which is exactly the regime in which the instrument is used to measure a wavelength.
questions.hint: The light travels to the moving mirror and back, so the path changes by twice the movement.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Measuring a wavelength with an interferometer
questions.learningObjective: recover a wavelength from a fringe count and a mirror movement
questions.stem: A Michelson interferometer is used with light of unknown wavelength. Moving one mirror 0.0750 mm causes 250 fringes to pass the detector. What is the wavelength, in nanometres? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Inverting the relation just used, the wavelength is twice the mirror movement over the number of fringes, so it is 2 x 7.50e-5 / 250 = 600 nm. The check is the mirror image of the calculation: 250 fringes of 600 nm require a two-way path change of 250 x 600e-9 = 1.50e-4 m, and that is exactly twice the 0.0750 mm moved, since 2 x 7.50e-5 = 1.50e-4. A second plausibility check is the colour. 600 nm lies in the orange, and a laboratory sodium lamp at 589 nm would give 255 fringes over that movement, so a few per cent of slack in the count is what a hand-counted fringe run would show. The method is the reason the wavelength of light can be quoted to seven figures, since the fringe count can be made large by moving the mirror far, and the only limit is the length of the moving rail.
questions.hint: Invert the previous relation: the path change is twice the movement and equals the fringe count times the wavelength.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why one mirror gives twice the path change
questions.learningObjective: explain that an interferometer path changes twice the movement of one mirror
questions.stem: In a two-beam interferometer with one fixed mirror and one on a sliding mount, a fringe passes for each wavelength of change in optical path difference. Why does moving the sliding mirror by d change the path difference by 2 d?

options.text: Because the light passes through the beam splitter twice on its way out to the mirror
options.misconception: attributes the doubling to a splitter passage, which both beams share

options.text: Because the beam splitter reflects the beam on the return journey, doubling the path
options.misconception: puts the doubling at the splitter rather than in the round trip to the mirror

options.text: Because the light travels to the moving mirror and back, so the route lengthens on both legs
Because the wavelength in the gap between the mirrors halves on the return journey
options.misconception: invents a change of wavelength, since the medium on both legs is the same air

questions.explanation: Each beam leaves the splitter, reaches a mirror and returns, so every point on the moving mirror is at the end of a round trip. Sliding that mirror outwards by d pushes the reflection point d further away on the way out and the beam has to travel d further back as well, and the two changes are in the same sense as far as the path difference is concerned. That is the whole reason, and it is geometric rather than optical: nothing about the wavelength, the medium or the beam splitter changes, only the length of the route. It is also why a moving mirror of d changes the interference condition the same way as moving the other mirror by 2 d, and why a mirror tilted by one wavelength of displacement produces a whole ring of fringes sweeping outwards rather than a displacement of the whole pattern. Once the factor of two is established it belongs in the instrument's calibration permanently, and forgetting it is the classic error in reading a fringe count.
questions.hint: Count the legs of the journey between the splitter and the mirror that is being moved.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Free spectral range of a Fabry-Perot etalon
questions.learningObjective: find the spacing between Fabry-Perot resonances from the mirror separation
questions.stem: Two parallel mirrors are set 0.100 mm apart with air between them, and light is admitted through a small hole in one of them. Taking the speed of light as 3.0e8 m per second, what is the frequency spacing between successive transmitted resonances, in hertz? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Successive resonances occur when the round trip between the mirrors adds one whole wavelength, so the spacing in frequency is one over the time light takes for a round trip, which is 2 d over c. With d = 1.0e-4 m that time is 2.0e-4 / 3.0e8 = 6.67e-13 s, and its reciprocal is 1.5e12 Hz. The same answer comes from the wavelength form, lambda = lambda over 2 n d, and the two agree because the time route and the frequency route are the same statement. Expressed in wavelength at 600 nm the spacing is 1.8 nm, since a frequency spacing of 1.5e12 near 600 nm corresponds to a small wavelength interval. The plausibility check is the round trip itself: the light makes the journey in under a picosecond, so the resonances are spaced by a terahertz rather than by a convenient laboratory frequency, which is the reason such a device is used to select a very narrow slice of a continuum rather than to produce a single useful line.
questions.hint: Resonances recur each time the round trip gains one whole wavelength, so work out the round-trip time.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Finesse of a Fabry-Perot etalon
questions.learningObjective: compute the finesse of a Fabry-Perot from the mirror reflectivity
questions.stem: The two mirrors of a Fabry-Perot etalon each reflect 90 per cent of the light reaching them. What is the finesse of the etalon, the ratio of the spacing between its resonances to the width of each one? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The finesse of the Airy transmission pattern is pi times the square root of the mirror reflectivity divided by one minus that reflectivity, and with a reflectivity of 0.90 that is pi x 0.9487 / 0.10, which is 29.8. The independent route is to evaluate the transmission itself. The Airy function is one over one plus a coefficient times the square of the sine of half the phase, with that coefficient being 4 R over (1 - R) squared, which is 360 here, and the half-maximum point then falls at a phase of 0.105 rad from a peak, so the full width is 0.211 rad out of the 2 pi between peaks. That ratio is 2 pi over 0.211, which is 29.8, the same figure. A finesse near 30 for 90 per cent mirrors is what published tables give, and it is worth noticing how sharply it depends on the reflectivity: raising it to 0.99 gives a finesse of 313, so the last few per cent of reflectivity buy an order of magnitude. That is the design lever behind high-finesse devices.
questions.hint: Use the finesse formula for the Airy pattern, then check it by finding where the transmission falls to half its peak.

questions.topic: Width of a Fabry-Perot resonance
questions.learningObjective: obtain the width of a Fabry-Perot resonance from the spacing and the finesse
questions.stem: A Fabry-Perot etalon with air 0.100 mm between its mirrors, each mirror reflecting 90 per cent of the light reaching it, is used with light of wavelength 600 nm. Taking the speed of light as 3.0e8 m per second, what is the full width at half maximum of a single transmitted resonance, in hertz? Report the number only.

options.text: 1.50e12 Hz, which is the spacing between the resonances and not their width
options.misconception: quotes the free spectral range where the half-maximum width belongs

options.text: 5.03e10 Hz, from the spacing between the resonances over the finesse
3.00e12 Hz, from a spacing computed as c over d rather than c over 2 d
options.misconception: uses the one-way gap instead of the round trip, doubling the spacing

options.text: 1.35e12 Hz, from multiplying the spacing by the mirror reflectivity instead of dividing
options.misconception: multiplies by the reflectivity where the finesse should divide the spacing

questions.explanation: The spacing between resonances is c over 2 n d, which with c = 3.0e8 and d = 1.0e-4 m is 1.5e12 Hz, and dividing that by the finesse of 29.8 gives the width, 1.5e12 / 29.8 = 5.0329e+10 Hz. The result is a small fraction of the spacing, which is the whole point of the device: a filter that passes 50 GHz out of every 1500 GHz available. Expressed in wavelength at 600 nm the same width is 6.0e-11 m, since a frequency width w at wavelength lambda corresponds to a wavelength width of w lambda squared over c, and 6.0e-11 m is a small fraction of a nanometre, far finer than a diffraction grating can work. That contrast is the reason an etalon is used for spectral selection in lasers and for locking a laser to a reference, while a grating, which is limited by the number of lines it has, is used where a broader slice will do.
questions.hint: The width is the spacing between resonances divided by the finesse.

options.text: Light that misses the direct route goes round many times, so many beams add at the exit

questions.explanation: The name describes the arithmetic of the interference. A two-beam instrument, such as the Michelson arrangement, adds exactly two contributions, and the resulting fringes are the familiar gentle cosines. Between two partly reflecting mirrors, each beam that is not transmitted is reflected back into the cavity, and the next bounce produces another contribution at the exit, and the next, and so on. With 90 per cent reflectivity there are of the order of thirty significant contributions, and the sum of many beams is a much sharper function than the sum of two, which is where the large finesse comes from. The energy bookkeeping is worth noticing: what is not transmitted on one pass is not lost but returned to the cavity, so the peaks of the pattern rise while the troughs between them fall. Two features follow from the large number of beams that do not hold for a two-beam device at all, namely a peak transmission close to unity and a width far narrower than the spacing.

The independent check is the round-trip time: 2.0e-4 / 3.0e8 = 6.67e-13 s, and its reciprocal is 1.5e12 Hz. Two ways of seeing why the factor of two cannot be omitted. If a resonance is a round-trip condition, changing the gap by d/2 changes the round trip by d and so moves the pattern by half a spacing, which is only consistent if the spacing itself is c over 2 d; and at 1.5e12 Hz the resonance spacing in wavelength near 600 nm is 1.8 nm, which is the sort of separation a 0.1 mm cavity actually gives, whereas 3.6 nm would require the light to make only one pass between successive resonances.

questions.topic: Why a broad source blurs an interference pattern
questions.learningObjective: explain that an extended source superposes shifted fringe patterns
questions.stem: A double slit gives a crisp fringe pattern under a single narrow source and a featureless blur under an ordinary lamp. What is different about the two cases?

options.misconception: invents a colour requirement, since a broad spectrum does not stop interference

options.text: Nothing is different, but the fringes move about far too quickly to be seen
options.misconception: claims a purely observational problem, whereas the contrast is genuinely lost

options.text: Each point of the lamp produces its own shifted pattern, and a wide source blurs them
The lamp is too dim, so the dark parts of the pattern cannot be seen at all
options.misconception: blames brightness, whereas a brighter broad source still gives a poor pattern

questions.explanation: The extended source is the issue, not the brightness or the colour. Every point of the lamp sends light to the two slits along a slightly different pair of directions, and each of those produces a complete fringe pattern displaced sideways by an amount proportional to the angular size of that piece of source. The screen therefore shows the sum of many such patterns at different displacements, and because the displacements are unrelated to each other the bright parts of one fall on the dark parts of another. The dark parts cancel first, because cancellation is more sensitive to misregistration than addition, and the pattern fades from the dark fringes outward until only a uniform brightness is left. That is why a lamp has to be confined to a narrow slit placed in the plane of the two slits, so that all the light reaching them comes from effectively one direction. Nothing about interference requires a single colour, and a bright enough extended source still gives a poor pattern.
questions.hint: Treat the source as a collection of separate point sources, each of which makes a whole pattern.

That gives lambda squared over delta lambda, or (550e-9) squared over 0.30e-9 = 3.025e-13 / 3.0e-10 = 1.008e-3 m, that is 1.01 mm. The independent route works in frequency. The spread in frequency is c times the spread in wavelength over the wavelength squared, 3.0e8 x 0.30e-9 / 3.025e-13 = 2.975e+11 Hz, and the coherence length is c over that, 3.0e8 / 2.98e11 = 1.008e-3 m again. The plausibility check is the sensitivity. Narrowing the filter to a spread of 0.06 nm, five times finer, would raise the coherence length fivefold to about 5.0 mm, and a source with a spread of a thousandth of a nanometre would reach metres, which is why a laser, whose light is nearly monochromatic, interferes across a laboratory. The formula is also quadratic in wavelength, so red light holds together four times longer than violet.
questions.hint: The coherence length is the wavelength multiplied by the number of wavelengths in the wave train.

options.misconception: denies that they are different requirements, though both concern phase relationships

questions.explanation: Temporal coherence asks whether a wave keeps a fixed phase relationship with a delayed version of itself, which is the requirement in a path-difference interferometer where the two beams travel unequal routes. It is a property of the bandwidth of the light, and the coherence length that follows is the reason a narrow filter is fitted in front of a broad source. Spatial coherence asks whether two different points on one wavefront have a fixed phase relationship, which is the requirement when light is split between two separated slits, and it is a property of how small the source is compared with the direction from which the light arrives. The two are independent in principle, and an experiment can be arranged to fail on either alone: a single-mode laser has excellent spatial coherence and a very long temporal coherence, while a wide slit destroys the spatial coherence of even perfectly monochromatic light. Keeping them apart is what makes it possible to say which remedy to apply to a washed-out pattern.

questions.learningObjective: compute fringe visibility from the amplitudes of two interfering beams

options.misconception: treats amplitudes as though they were intensities, which halves the answer

options.misconception: references the contrast to the stronger beam alone rather than to the mean

The bounds are the check: visibility cannot exceed 1, it falls to 0 when one beam is absent or when the two are completely uncorrelated, and 0.80 is comfortably inside that, corresponding to an imperfectly balanced interferometer in which some light has been lost or polarised out of one arm.

The line spacing is the reciprocal of the density, 1 over 6.0e5 m, that is 1.667e-6 m, and at 500 nm in the second order the sine is 0.6, so the cosine is 0.8 and the dispersion is 2 over (1.667e-6 x 0.8) = 1.500e+6 radians per metre. The same figure comes from the density directly, since m over d is just m times the line density, giving 2 x 6.0e5 divided by 0.8, which is the same number. The cosine in the denominator is the point of the exercise: dispersion improves as an order is used at a larger angle, so a grating used in the blaze order gains nothing from the extra angular spread unless it is already operating far from the normal. In more familiar units the figure is 1.5e-3 radians, or 309 arcseconds, per nanometre of wavelength, which is a large spread and is why a grating disperses more than a prism at comparable size.

options.misconception: calls 0.61 a rounding of one half, which would be a 22 per cent error

The group index is the derivative of that, the rate at which the index changes with wavelength, and it fixes how fast the crest of a pulse and the rest of the band around it travel, which is the group velocity. The two are equal only in the ideal case of a medium whose index does not vary with wavelength, and they differ wherever a medium is dispersive, which is essentially everywhere in the visible. The distinction is not academic. A pulse crossing a dispersive medium emerges with its crest arriving at the group velocity while its oscillation continues at the phase velocity, and the two facts are what produce the spreading of a pulse and the broadening of a spectral line, both of which matter in optical communications.

The sign is the physical check. In normal dispersion the index falls with wavelength, so the slope is negative and the group index is larger than the phase index, which is what makes the group velocity slower than the phase velocity; an anomalous region, where the index rises with wavelength, would put the group index below the phase index. questions.stem: Glass and most transparent solids are described as having normal dispersion, while some wavelength regions near absorption bands are described as anomalous. What distinguishes the two?

options.text: Normal dispersion means the index rises with wavelength, which is what a prism uses
options.misconception: reverses the definition, since normal dispersion has the index falling as the wavelength grows

options.text: Anomalous dispersion means the index is constant, so a lens shows no colour at all
options.misconception: calls a zero slope anomalous, whereas anomalous means the slope has the other sign

options.text: Normal dispersion occurs in glass, and anomalous dispersion occurs only in gases
options.misconception: restricts anomalous dispersion to gases, whereas it appears in dense materials too

options.text: Normal dispersion has the index falling with wavelength; anomalous has it rising

questions.explanation: The two cases are the two signs of the slope of the index against wavelength. Normal dispersion, the index falling as the wavelength rises, is the rule in transparent regions and is what makes a prism spread a white beam into a spectrum, red being deviated least and violet most. Typical values for crown glass are an index of 1.514 at 486 nm falling to 1.489 at 656 nm, a drop of 0.025 across 170 nm, which is a slope of the order of 1.5e-4 per nanometre and the figure used in the previous two calculations. Anomalous dispersion appears close to an absorption band, where the index rises with wavelength, and it is normal for a material near a resonance. The distinction carries a consequence that sounds paradoxical and is worth stating: in an anomalous region the group velocity exceeds the phase velocity and can exceed the speed of light in vacuum, and no information has travelled faster than light, because the group velocity describes the peak of a pulse in a strongly absorbing, strongly dispersive material rather than a signal being carried at that speed.
questions.hint: Compare the slope of the index against wavelength in the two cases, and use a familiar pair of values to fix the sign.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Brewster angle for a given index
questions.learningObjective: compute the Brewster angle from the ratio of the two refractive indices
questions.stem: Light passes from air into a material of refractive index 1.600. At what angle to the normal is the reflected beam free of any light whose electric field lies in the plane of incidence? Give the answer in degrees only.
questions.explanation: That condition is the Brewster angle, and it is fixed by the ratio of the indices through the tangent of the angle, so the angle is the arctangent of 1.600, which is 58.0 degrees. Two independent checks are available and both are worth doing. First, at the Brewster angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular, so the sine of the angle of incidence is n over the square root of 1 plus n squared, which is 1.600 / 1.8868 = 0.848, and the arctangent of 0.848 over 0.530 is again 58.0 degrees. Second, Snell's law must return the same index: with the refracted angle the complement of 58.0 degrees, the ratio of the sines is 0.848 over 0.530 = 1.600. The magnitude is the plausibility check: the angle always exceeds 45 degrees and grows with the index, so glass at 1.50 gives 56.3 degrees and a denser material at 1.60 gives the 58.0 degrees here, while a material barely denser than air would give an angle only just above 45 degrees.
questions.hint: The tangent of the angle is the ratio of the indices; then check it against the perpendicular-ray condition.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Polarization produced by reflection at the Brewster angle
questions.learningObjective: explain that reflection at the Brewster angle leaves only one field direction
questions.stem: At the angle at which no light is reflected with its electric field in the plane of incidence, what is the state of polarization of the reflected beam?

options.text: Unpolarized, since only half of the light reaches that direction
options.misconception: describes the transmitted beam, which is only partially polarized at that angle

options.text: Fully polarized, with the field perpendicular to the plane of incidence
Fully polarized, with the field in the plane of incidence
options.misconception: picks the component that was not reflected at all, so the beam cannot contain it

options.text: Both beams fully polarized, since one beam can have only one plane
options.misconception: polarizes the transmitted beam too, which it is not at that angle

questions.explanation: The reflection coefficient of the electric field lying in the plane of incidence passes smoothly through zero at the Brewster angle, so at that setting not one photon with that field direction is reflected and none can appear in the outgoing beam. What does appear is the other component, the one perpendicular to the plane of incidence, and a beam containing only one field direction is by definition fully polarized. The transmitted beam at the same angle is only partially polarized, with a surplus of the in-plane component, since the in-plane light is being preferentially transmitted rather than reflected. This is the principle behind the simplest polarizer ever made: a rod of glass or a sheet of mica is rotated about its axis to sweep the angle of incidence, and at one setting the surface reflection vanishes and the only light leaving the end is a single plane of polarization. The angle for ordinary glass is the arctangent of 1.50, that is 56.3 degrees, which is close to the 57 degrees a rod makes with its own axis.
questions.hint: One component of the field is not reflected at all at that angle, so ask what the surviving beam can contain.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Index recovered from a measured Brewster angle
questions.learningObjective: recover a refractive index from a measured angle of zero polarized reflection
questions.stem: Light is reflected from the flat surface of a transparent solid, and the reflected beam is found to have no component in the plane of incidence when the angle of incidence is 56.3 degrees. Taking the tangent of 56.3 degrees as 1.499, what is the refractive index of the solid relative to air? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The measurement is of the Brewster angle, so the index follows directly as the tangent of that angle multiplied by the index of the medium the light came from, which here is air at 1, giving 1 x 1.499 = 1.499. The independent route uses the perpendicular-ray condition. At that angle the refracted ray leaves the reflected one at 90 degrees, so the angle inside the solid is 33.7 degrees, and Snell's law requires the ratio of the sines of the two angles to be the index: 0.8320 over 0.5548 is 1.499, the same figure. The direction of the check is the point, since an instrument reading an angle does not carry a tangent table, so recovering the index through Snell's law is the practical form of the calculation. The plausibility check is the identity of the material: an index of about 1.50 is ordinary crown glass, and returning it to a tangent gives back 56.3 degrees, so the round trip closes.
questions.hint: Either take the tangent of the measured angle, or use the perpendicular condition with Snell's law.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Reflectance at normal incidence
questions.learningObjective: compute the reflected fraction at a boundary from the two refractive indices
questions.stem: Light travels from air into glass of refractive index 1.500 and is reflected at normal incidence. What fraction of the incident intensity is reflected? Report the number only.

options.text: 0.20, from the ratio of the difference to the sum of the two indices
options.misconception: omits the square, which is what turns a field ratio into an intensity ratio

options.text: 0.667, from the ratio of the smaller index to the larger one
options.misconception: quotes an index ratio, which is neither the field nor the intensity reflection

options.text: 0.040, from the square of the ratio of the difference to the sum of the two indices
0.020, from halving the square as though there were one interface of half the weight
options.misconception: divides the answer by two on a mistaken symmetry argument

questions.explanation: At normal incidence the reflected fraction of the intensity is the square of the ratio of the difference of the two indices to their sum, and with 1.000 and 1.500 that is 0.500 over 2.500, squared, giving 0.040. The square is the essential step, since the expression without it, 0.20, is a field amplitude ratio and not an intensity ratio. The energy check is exact and worth doing: the transmitted fraction is 1 - R = 0.96, so the two sum to one, as they must at a boundary with no absorption. The independent route through the transmission coefficient agrees, since the field amplitude transmitted is 2 n1 over n1 plus n2, that is 0.8, whose square is 0.64, and correcting for the ratio of the indices across the boundary multiplies that by 1.500 to give 0.96. The magnitude is plausible too: 4 per cent from one surface of ordinary glass, 8 per cent from a plain slab with two surfaces, and 17 per cent from a surface of diamond whose index of 2.42 gives (1.42 over 3.42) squared.
questions.hint: The intensity reflection is the square of a field ratio, and the two must add up to one.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why glass reflects so little at normal incidence
questions.learningObjective: explain that a small index mismatch produces a small reflected fraction
questions.stem: A ray of light strikes ordinary glass at normal incidence and only 4 per cent of its intensity is reflected, even though the glass is a solid. Why is the reflected fraction so small?

options.text: Only a small mismatch between the two indices means only a small field mismatch to reflect
Glass is thin, so the light has not had time to reflect from its second surface
options.misconception: explains the low total, but the 4 per cent is from the first surface alone

options.text: Glass is transparent, and a transparent material cannot reflect light at all
options.misconception: confuses transparency with zero reflection, which contradicts the 4 per cent given

options.text: The reflected wave is cancelled by the light returning from the back of the glass
options.misconception: requires a second surface and an interference effect that is not present here

questions.explanation: The reflected field is proportional to the mismatch between the indices on the two sides of the boundary, and for glass the mismatch is small: 1.500 against 1.000 gives a ratio of 0.500 over 2.500, that is 0.2, and the intensity is the square of that, 0.04. A material whose index matched its surroundings exactly would reflect nothing at all, and a material with a much higher index reflects a great deal, which is why diamond at 2.42 reflects 17 per cent from each surface and why water at 1.33, reflecting 2 per cent, is so much less reflective than glass. So transparency and reflectivity are not opposites: a transparent material can reflect several per cent, which is why camera lenses are coated to suppress it. The second option is a real effect on the total figure, since a thin film returns light from its back surface and can raise the total to about 8 per cent, but it does not touch the 4 per cent being asked about, and the last option describes an interference that would apply only if the two reflections overlapped coherently.
questions.hint: Ask how much the refractive index changes across the boundary, and how the reflected fraction depends on that change.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Retardation produced by a wave plate
questions.learningObjective: compute the phase retardation of a wave plate from its thickness and index difference
questions.stem: A wave plate is 20 micrometres thick and the difference between its two principal refractive indices is 0.0050. Light of wavelength 500 nm in air passes through it at normal incidence. What phase difference, in degrees, does the plate introduce between the two components? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The two components travel different optical path lengths through the plate, and the difference is the thickness times the index difference, 20e-6 x 0.0050 = 1.0e-7 m, which is 0.2 of the 500 nm wavelength. A path difference of a fifth of a wavelength is a phase difference of 0.2 of a full turn, that is 0.2 x 360 = 72 degrees. The two routes agree: expressing the path difference as a fraction of the wavelength gives 1.0e-7 over 5.0e-7 = 0.2, and multiplying by 360 gives the same 72 degrees. The size is the plausibility check. A wave plate works because the optical path difference it introduces is a fraction of a wavelength, so the two components emerge nearly in step and a plate 20 micrometres thick in a material of index difference 0.0050 gives an optical path of 100 nanometres, which is a fifth of a wavelength, as required. For comparison a quarter-wave plate of the same material would need to be 25 micrometres thick, and a half-wave plate 50, so a plate of 20 micrometres is four fifths of the way to a quarter-wave plate and delivers four fifths of a quarter turn.
questions.hint: Find the optical path difference, express it as a fraction of a wavelength, and convert that fraction to degrees.

questions.topic: Thickness of a quarter-wave plate
questions.learningObjective: size a wave plate for a quarter-wave retardation at a given wavelength
questions.stem: A wave plate is to be cut so that it is a quarter-wave plate for light of wavelength 500 nm in air, and the difference between its two principal refractive indices is 0.0050. What thickness, in micrometres, is required? Report the number only.

options.text: 1.00 micrometre, from a hundred in place of four in the denominator
options.misconception: replaces the four by a hundred, making the plate a hundred times too thin

options.text: 25.0 micrometres, from the wavelength over four times the index difference
50.0 micrometres, from two in place of four in the denominator
options.misconception: gives a half-wave plate, since two halves of a wavelength make a whole one

options.text: 12.5 micrometres, from halving the wavelength before dividing by the index difference
options.misconception: halves the wavelength before dividing, though the condition calls for the full wavelength

questions.explanation: A quarter-wave plate has to add a quarter of a wavelength of optical path, so the thickness times the index difference is the wavelength over four, and the thickness is 5.0e-7 / (4 x 0.0050) = 2.5e-5 m, that is 25.0 micrometres. The check is to put the thickness back: 0.0050 x 2.5e-5 = 1.25e-7 m, which is exactly a quarter of 5.0e-7 m. It also sits in the family, since the same material gives a half-wave plate at twice this thickness, 50.0 micrometres, which is the third option and a plate that adds half a wavelength rather than a quarter. That pair in turn fixes the plate considered in the previous item: a 20 micrometre plate is four fifths of a quarter-wave plate, and 0.8 of 90 degrees is 72 degrees, the retardation calculated there. The magnitudes are the plausibility check, since a few tens of micrometres is exactly the thickness of the crystalline plates used in practice.
questions.hint: Set the optical path difference, thickness times index difference, equal to a quarter of a wavelength.

questions.topic: Rotation of polarization by a half-wave plate
questions.learningObjective: state that a half-wave plate turns polarization to twice the angle from its axis
questions.stem: A half-wave plate is placed in a beam whose electric field lies at 20 degrees to the plate's own fast axis. In what direction does the field emerge from the plate?

options.text: At 20 degrees from the fast axis, since the plate does not move the axis of polarization
options.misconception: ignores the reversal that the half-wave retardation produces

options.text: At 10 degrees from the fast axis, since the plate halves the angle it is given
options.misconception: halves the input angle instead of doubling it, the opposite of what the plate does

options.text: At 90 degrees from the fast axis, whatever the incoming polarization was
options.misconception: makes the rotation independent of the input, which is the one case it is not

options.text: At 40 degrees from the fast axis, since the angle is reflected about that axis

questions.explanation: The half-wave retardation leaves the two components of the field exactly half a cycle out of step, which is the same as reversing the sign of one of them, and reversing one component of a vector reflects it about the axis along which the other lies. An input at 20 degrees to the fast axis therefore leaves at 40 degrees to it, and the general rule is that the emerging direction makes twice the input angle with the axis. The two extremes confirm the rule. Along the fast axis, an angle of zero, the field emerges along it unchanged, and 0 doubled is 0; along the slow axis, an angle of 90 degrees, it emerges along that axis with its sign reversed, and 90 degrees doubled is 180 degrees, which is the same direction turned inside out. That makes the plate a controllable rotator, and rotating the plate by a known angle rotates the polarization by twice that amount, which is how the polarization of a beam is trimmed to a chosen direction without absorbing any of it.
questions.hint: A half cycle of retardation reverses one component, and reversing a component reflects the direction about the other axis.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why a shorter wavelength improves resolving power
questions.learningObjective: explain the wavelength and aperture scaling that sets an instrument's resolution
questions.stem: A designer can raise the resolving power of an optical instrument either by enlarging its aperture or by shortening the wavelength it uses. Explain, from the diffraction argument, why each change helps, and state the scaling law that relates the smallest resolved separation to the aperture and the wavelength.

answer.exemplar: Start from the image of a point, not from the object. A point object does not form a point image: the aperture admits a range of directions, the waves arriving from different points of the aperture travel different distances, and the field in the image therefore has a finite angular size. Two points closer together than that size are imaged as a single patch, and no amount of magnification separates them, because magnification enlarges both images at once. That size is the diffraction limit, and for a circular aperture of diameter D the angular radius of the first dark ring is 1.22 wavelengths over D, while the smallest resolvable separation is of that order. Put the wavelength in place of the separation to get the two standard cases. For a telescope, where the quantity of interest is an angle, the resolved angle falls as 1.22 lambda over D, so doubling the aperture halves the smallest angle and shortening the wave by a factor of two does the same. For a microscope, where the quantity of interest is a distance on the specimen, the same argument with the acceptance half-angle gives 0.61 lambda over the numerical aperture, so again the limit is directly proportional to the wavelength and inversely proportional to the aperture. Both scalings follow from the same arithmetic, a ratio of a length of wavelength to a length of aperture, so neither improvement is a matter of technique. Two checks confirm the reasoning. The scaling is consistent across instruments: at 500 nm an aperture of 1.00 m resolves 0.013 arcseconds and a 0.10 m aperture resolves 0.13, a factor of ten in each direction, and the ultraviolet, working at 100 nm, gains a further factor of five over the visible for the same aperture, which is the whole reason ultraviolet microscopes see what visible ones cannot. And the balance is sharp: visible light at 1.00 m and ultraviolet at 0.20 m resolve about the same detail, so gaining a factor of five in wavelength has cost a factor of five in aperture, and it is the product of the two that the ratio depends on. There is a limit to this, since the aperture cannot be enlarged indefinitely and the wavelength cannot be shortened indefinitely, and the shortest usable wavelength is set by the absorption of the material the instrument is made from, which is why extreme ultraviolet and X-ray instruments need evacuated paths and different optics altogether.

questions.explanation: A point object is imaged as a small disc because the aperture admits a range of directions and the contributions from different points of the aperture travel different distances, so the two elements of the answer follow from the size of that disc and nothing else. The disc's angular size is 1.22 wavelengths over the aperture for a circular stop, so it is proportional to the wavelength and inversely proportional to the aperture, which means shortening the wave and enlarging the stop each improve the limit by exactly the factor by which they are changed. Neither improvement is a matter of technique or of instrument quality, and the same statement covers a telescope, where the quantity is an angle, and a microscope, where it is 0.61 wavelengths over the numerical aperture, since both come from the ratio of a wavelength to an aperture. The cost is worth noting: the limit depends on the product of the two, so an ultraviolet instrument gains little for the same aperture and ultraviolet optics are expensive.
questions.hint: Begin with why a point source is imaged as a small disc, and write the disc size before discussing what improves it.
